title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media. An AI-generated video of a well-known figure from the financial sector was used as an advertisement for an investment promising large returns, and the person who saw it treated the face and voice as evidence that the offer was real. The AI did not take the money. It supplied the credibility that made the approach worth answering.

The impersonation sat at the very front of the fraud, in the advertising that recruited the victim. Everything after it was ordinary tradecraft: a small initial investment, contact moved to WhatsApp, pressure to pay more, help opening online accounts, remote access to the victim's computer, encouragement to borrow. The PSNI described the operation as a sophisticated and substantial fraud, and BBC News NI has seen comparable scams built on the images of named financial experts. Catching it at the point of contact would have required confirming that the person in the video was actually connected to the investment, and checking Financial Conduct Authority authorisation, which is what police advised people to do.

What is not established is who the figure in the video was, since the PSNI did not name them, and whether that person had any knowledge of or involvement in the scam. No arrest, charge or court finding is reported, and the loss figure comes from the police account rather than from a concluded case.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 after scammers used an AI generated video of a well known financial sector figure to advertise an investment that promised large returns, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said. The PSNI did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI has seen similar scams using financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. After a small initial investment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more.

Police said the fraudsters persuaded the victim to open several online accounts and gave them remote access to their computer, claiming to help with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. The PSNI called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. Superintendent Joanne Gibson of the Scamwise Partnership urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised verifying who people are dealing with and checking Financial Conduct Authority authorization where appropriate.
title_en: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity
